outcomes.text: Distinguish a verb complement from a VP adjunct and explain where it attaches.
Distinguish a particle from a preposition and an understood complement from an optional detail.
Distinguish an event adverbial from a sentence adverbial by what it modifies.

opening.prompt: In “The nurse checked the chart at noon”, which group tells when the check happened?

options.feedback: The chart is what the nurse checked.
This PP tells when the checking happened.
This group names the activity itself.

opening.prompt: In “Ari put the key on the hook”, which group tells where the key ended up?

options.feedback: Ari is the person who moved the key.
The key is the thing Ari moved.
This PP gives the resulting location of the key.

opening.prompt: Replace “the light” with “it” in “Sal switched off the light”. Which version keeps the original meaning?

options.feedback: The object pronoun comes before the particle.
In this switching pattern the pronoun precedes “off”.
This leaves out the particle that gives the switching-off meaning.

opening.prompt: Mina is giving class handouts to Ren. Someone says “Mina gave two copies”. Who is understood to receive them?

options.feedback: Mina is the giver.
The context identifies Ren as the recipient.
“Two copies” names what was given.

opening.prompt: In “Luckily, the glass stayed intact”, what does “luckily” express?

options.feedback: The statement describes what happened to the glass. “Luckily” evaluates the outcome.
The word gives no time for the event.

options.text: The speaker’s evaluation of what happened
options.feedback: The speaker presents the whole outcome as fortunate.

closing.prompt: In “Lea scrubbed the pan after dinner, and Nia did so before lunch”, what does “did so” stand for?

options.feedback: Include what was scrubbed in the activity that both people did.
The time changes while the verb and its object stay together.
Nia did the activity before lunch. The first time phrase is outside the replaced group.

closing.prompt: In “Nia put the crate under the stairs”, where does “under the stairs” attach?

options.text: Beside V and the object NP in the basic VP
options.feedback: The PP completes the placement pattern and locates the crate.

options.text: Beside the basic VP in a higher VP
options.feedback: An optional event detail would attach there. This PP supplies the resulting location of the object.
“Nia” is the subject. The PP belongs inside the predicate.

closing.prompt: In “Ari folded it up”, what is “up” doing?

options.feedback: A preposition heads a phrase with a following complement here. “It” is the object of “folded”.
“Up” contributes to the meaning of the folding, inside the predicate.

options.text: Serving as the particle of “fold up”
options.feedback: The particle follows the object pronoun in the separated form.

closing.prompt: Ari is giving things to Jo. Someone says “Ari gave a ticket”. What does E represent in the tree for this use?

options.feedback: “A ticket” is overt. E marks the role that context fills.
Jo receives the ticket. That role is understood even though no words name Jo.
No time is implied by E. The context supplies the recipient.

closing.prompt: In “Unfortunately, the lamp broke”, what does “unfortunately” attach beside?

options.text: The S “the lamp broke”, under a higher S
options.feedback: The word gives the speaker’s evaluation of the whole statement.

options.text: The V “broke”, within the basic VP
options.feedback: “Unfortunately” gives an evaluation of the event rather than a complement of the verb.

options.text: The noun “lamp”, within the subject NP
options.feedback: The evaluation applies to what happened, rather than identifying the lamp.
